kurz: The five phases of a speculative bubble, and the credit that distinguishes a bubble from a market that is merely expensive.

bloecke.md:
A bubble is a financing phenomenon. High prices can also arise because many people are optimistic. Such an exaggeration corrects itself quietly over years, without headlines. A market only becomes dangerous when a large part of the purchases is paid for with borrowed money. The timing of the sale is then determined by the loan agreement and no longer by the investor's own judgement.

From this, Hyman Minsky developed a theory of financial instability in the 1970s. According to this theory, stability makes market participants careless, and this carelessness in turn brings the stability to an end. In 1978, Charles Kindleberger applied the model to the financial crises from 1720 up to the 1970s and divided the course of bubbles into five phases. The result is a classification scheme. It helps to place a current market, but it cannot say when the turnaround will come. Therein lie both the use and the limit of the model.

## Displacement (phase 1)

It starts with good news. An external shock changes profit expectations in a credible way. Examples are the end of a war, a technology that becomes usable, the deregulation of a market, a sharp fall in interest rates or a large inflow of money into a country. Kindleberger calls this trigger *displacement*, that is, a shift.

Most accounts of bubbles pass over the fact that the story behind them is usually true. Tulip bulbs were scarce, the internet has changed the world, and Japan achieved high export surpluses. What was inflated in each case was the price paid for it. You therefore cannot recognise a bubble by the fact that the underlying idea is nonsense.

A textbook example from Germany is less well known than the big cases. After 1871, an inflow of money from abroad met rules on company formation that had only just been relaxed. The 1870 amendment to company law (Aktienrechtsnovelle) had abolished the state licensing requirement for joint-stock companies and replaced it with a system of statutory requirements (Normativsystem). From then on, meeting the legal requirements was enough to found a company.

bloecke.titel: The five phases in the founders' crash (Gründerkrach), 1871-1874
bloecke.unter: Less than two years passed between the inflow of money and the first wave of bankruptcies, and the trigger came from Vienna, not from Berlin.

ereignisse.text: French reparations of 5 billion francs flow into the German Reich, around 2.5 to 3 billion of it into the capital market. Shortly before, the 1870 amendment to company law had abolished the licensing requirement.
928 joint-stock companies are founded in Prussia, compared with 88 in the previous four years. They are joined by 61 new banks that finance the issues themselves.
Share prices reach their peak. Companies continue to be founded, although the earnings of the young companies have long ceased to justify the issue prices.
The Vienna stock exchange collapses and is closed at 13:00. Within a few hours, more than 120 banks are insolvent.
The crisis reaches New York. Credit crises spread to where the same creditors are exposed, not to where the same goods are produced.
For 444 German companies, the price loss since December 1872 adds up to around 2 billion marks. The clean-up takes longer than the entire boom.

bloecke.md:
## Credit-financed boom (phase 2)

A boom becomes a bubble when the purchases are financed with loans. The mechanism is one of accounting, not psychology. When a bank grants a loan, it does not lend out existing savings deposits; it expands its balance sheet. It books the claim on the asset side and the loan amount as the customer's sight deposit on the liabilities side. The deposit is therefore a consequence of the loan and not its precondition. The Deutsche Bundesbank expressly clarified this in its Monthly Report of April 2017.

This can give rise to a feedback loop that drives prices independently of any valuation. New credit money is used to buy assets, whose prices rise as a result. Because the lending value that the bank recognises as collateral follows the market price, the same position can now carry more debt. The additional credit line is used for further purchases. As long as this loop continues, it looks like value creation. But it is balance sheet expansion.

bloecke.titel: The credit loop of a bubble and its breaking point
bloecke.unter: The individual steps are harmless in themselves; only the closed loop becomes dangerous, because it reinforces itself.

bloecke.md: Credit growth can be observed in official statistics. In July 2026, loans to the private sector in the euro area grew by 4.1% year on year, loans to households by 3.1% and loans to non-financial corporations by 4.4%. The money supply M3 rose by 3.4%. These rates are close to nominal economic growth and thus argue against a credit boom. Figures like these therefore belong at the start of any assessment of a possible bubble, even before prices. An expensive market without credit expansion corrects itself. A market that is only moderately expensive but has strong credit expansion, on the other hand, can collapse.

## The effect of leverage when prices fall

A calculation that needs no assumptions shows what difference credit makes. A position of €10,000 loses 20%. This price loss is the same for every investor. The consequences depend solely on what part of the position was paid for with borrowed money.

bloecke.titel: Position of €10,000, price fall of 20% (illustrative calculation, excluding interest and costs)
Equity in a €10,000 position after a 20% fall
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with the same position, the same price loss and different financing. From leverage of 5, the equity is used up; beyond that, a margin call falls due. With a securities-backed loan, the margin call comes even at lower leverage, because the lending value is below the market value.

bloecke.titel: Forced sale with a securities-backed loan
bloecke.md: With a German securities-backed or Lombard loan, the broker sets a lending value for each security and may lower it unilaterally. In crashes this happens, often for the very securities that are falling. If the collateral falls short of the required cover, a margin call follows, and after the deadline expires the institution sells the securities itself. The investor thus loses the ability to sit out a fall. It is only this ability that makes shares a long-term investment. Leverage therefore does not just amplify the return; above all, it shortens the time for which an investor can hold out through a fall.

## Euphoria (phase 3)

In the third phase, it is above all the justification for the prices that changes. Because the classic yardsticks no longer justify the prices, new ones are introduced, such as user numbers instead of profits, revenue multiples instead of the price-to-earnings ratio, or floor space instead of rental income. At the same time, the circle of buyers widens. People who had paid no attention to the market until then start buying. They buy because others have made money with it, not because they have checked a valuation.

One hallmark of this phase is the sentence “This time is different”. Carmen Reinhart and Kenneth Rogoff made it the title of their book on eight centuries of financial crises. Mostly it is even true, because circumstances have changed. But the solvency of debtors is governed by the same rules as always.

bloecke.md:
## Profit-taking and stagnation (phase 4)

This phase is the least conspicuous, but it is the most important. Insiders get out: founders sell stakes, existing shareholders place shares on the market and banks pass on credit risks. Prices therefore do not crash; they simply stop rising. Kindleberger calls this state *distress*. The market moves sideways although the news remains good, and the debt stays in the system unchanged.

The trigger of the downturn is almost always an ordinary event and rarely identical to the cause, for example a rate rise, a failed issue or an accounting scandal at a smaller listed company. The Bank of Japan raised its key interest rate from 2.5% to 6.0% between May 1989 and August 1990. That was a normal monetary tightening. It only had a devastating effect because prices had already risen very far beforehand. A market collapses as soon as no more buyers come. Bad news is not needed for that.

## Panic (phase 5)

In the panic, the credit loop reverses. Falling prices lower the lending values, lower lending values force sales, and these sales push prices down further. What gets sold is whatever can be sold, regardless of its quality. Investors who need liquidity part with their liquid and healthy positions. This is why correlations between different investments approach one in panics, as in 1987, 2008 and March 2020. Diversification thus systematically fails at the very moment it would be needed most.

Panics today unfold faster than in the past, but not more deeply. In the coronavirus crash, the S&P 500 lost 33.9% in 33 calendar days. The average bear market since 1950, by contrast, lasted 338 days to the trough, and on average considerably more time passed after that before the previous peak was regained. Institutions have long responded with the same tools: a lender of last resort and trading halts. The NYSE introduced its circuit breakers in 1988, one year after Black Monday.

More important than the level of valuation is what part of the price is borrowed and who will have to sell if the price falls by a fifth. The valuation determines the expected return. The debt determines whether a fall remains an ordinary correction.

## Warning signs and their limited use

Six characteristics can be observed on an ongoing basis: credit growth above income growth; new financing vehicles that circumvent rules; a wave of issues by companies without profits; valuation yardsticks that replace cash flow; broader participation by new investors; sales by insiders. The data on these are public and can be found in the statistics of central banks and stock exchanges.

What is difficult is determining the timing. The characteristics appear years before the peak, and during this time prices keep rising. In December 1996, Alan Greenspan spoke of “irrational exuberance”. But the Nasdaq Composite only reached its peak of 5,048.62 points on 10 March 2000, far above its level of December 1996. Investors who got out in 1996 were right on the substance but lost out economically.

In addition, there is the base rate, that is, the frequency of such declines. Since 1928, the S&P 500 has had around 100 declines of at least 10%, that is, around one a year on average, and since 1945 declines of 20% or more around every five years. If you got out after every warning signal, you would therefore not be invested most of the time. Moreover, around 76% of the best stock market days fall in a bear market or in the first two months after one.

In retrospect, every bubble looks obvious, because the end is known and the time before it has been forgotten. Contemporaries, on the other hand, almost never recognised a bubble. In October 1929, Irving Fisher saw share prices on a permanently high plateau. The claim “I would have sold in 1999” cannot be verified and is therefore no basis for a decision today.

Two schools of thought face each other in monetary policy here. One is traditionally represented by the Bank for International Settlements. It regards credit booms as the main problem and wants to counter them early (*lean against the wind*), even if this weakens growth without any acute reason. The other was long the line of the US Federal Reserve. It held that bubbles cannot be identified with certainty and that cleaning up the consequences after they burst is cheaper than precautionary tightening (*clean up afterwards*). The crisis from 2007 onwards weakened the second position without proving the first. An interest rate that stops a bubble also slows down the rest of the economy.

Since 2008, macroprudential supervision has been regarded as a compromise. Its instruments target credit rather than prices. In Germany, they are governed by the Banking Act (Kreditwesengesetz, KWG). They include the countercyclical capital buffer under Section 10d KWG, which is built up in good times and released in a crisis, and the systemic risk buffer under Section 10e KWG, which can be limited to individual sectors, such as residential mortgage loans. Whether this is enough remains open, because no buffer has yet been tested in a genuine asset price crisis.

The model is no use for timing, but it is useful for structuring your own portfolio:

- Debt-financed securities positions should be avoided as long as a fall of 20% could trigger a margin call. The table above shows why.
- Position size matters more than the forecast. For an investment with historical declines of 70% to 85%, the weighting determines the outcome, not the timing of the exit.
- The tax consequences should be calculated in advance. A loss from selling shares in a panic is booked to the share loss pot (Aktienverlusttopf). It can only be offset against gains from sales of shares under Section 20(6) sentence 4 EStG (Income Tax Act), not against income from funds, interest or certificates. The bank offsets it immediately against share gains of the same year, including those made earlier in the year, and carries the remainder forward to the following years (Section 43a(3) sentences 2 and 3 EStG). Investors who then only hold ETFs practically never use this remainder. It can only be offset across different securities accounts with a loss certificate (Verlustbescheinigung), which must be requested by 15 December of the year (Section 43a(3) sentence 5 EStG).

There is no recognised quantitative criterion that separates a bubble from a justified revaluation in real time. Every definition that works in retrospect produces false alarms when applied to the future. The phase model describes historical episodes and is not a tested theory with a hit rate.

mitnehmen: Whether an expensive market is a bubble depends on the share of borrowed money behind the purchases.
The story behind a bubble is almost always true; what is inflated is the price it is supposed to justify.
Credit creates a loop of rising prices and rising lending values that reverses in the panic and forces sales.
The warning signs of a bubble can be observed publicly, but they appear years before the peak and therefore help in choosing the position size, not in choosing the exit date.
Investors without loans can sit out every phase; investors with loans do not decide the timing of the sale themselves.

begriffe.text: The point at which leveraged investors have to sell assets to service their debts. The sales cause prices to fall further and force further sales.
The mutual reinforcement of credit expansion, rising asset prices, rising lending values and renewed credit expansion, and the reversal of this process in a crisis.
Loan from a bank or broker, secured by the borrower's own portfolio. The lending value of each security is set by the institution and can be lowered unilaterally.
Demand by the lender, after a price fall, for additional collateral or money. If it is not met, the institution sells the securities itself.
Supervisory instrument under Section 10d KWG (Banking Act). In times of strong credit growth, banks have to hold additional capital, which is released in a crisis.
